correctness.rationale: Sufficiency is given by direct nonnegative integer factorizations when \(c\mid n\) or \(b\mid n\). For necessity, \(A=RS\), \(B=SR\), and \(\det A\ne0\) force \(R\) and \(S\) nonsingular and hence \(AR=RB\). Writing \(R=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}\), the intertwining equations give \(q=br\) and \(s=cp\). Solving \(S=R^{-1}A\) yields nonnegative integers \(U,V\) with \(S=\begin{pmatrix}cV&bU\\U&V\end{pmatrix}\). The \((1,2)\) entry of \(RS=A\) gives \(pU+rV=1\), so one of the nonnegative integer products is one and the other zero. The \((1,1)\) entry then forces \(n=cp\) or \(n=br\), proving \(c\mid n\) or \(b\mid n\). Fresh bounded enumeration of the reduced intertwiner form for \(1\le n\le8\) and \(1\le b,c\le5\) found an elementary factorization exactly in the predicted divisibility cases.

value.rationale: Elementary SSE is the atomic move underlying strong shift equivalence, and recent work is explicitly constructing and shortening paths for difficult two-by-two examples. An exact all-parameter criterion identifying when a natural diagonal Baker-type family collapses to one step is therefore a motivated structural classification, with a simple divisibility obstruction that can guide path searches.
residual_risks: The theorem does not decide total SSE length when the elementary obstruction fires.

final_claim: For positive integers \(n,b,c\) with \(n^2\ne bc\), let \(A_{n;b,c}=\begin{pmatrix}n&b\\c&n\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B_{n;b,c}=\begin{pmatrix}n&bc\\1&n\end{pmatrix}\). These matrices are elementary strong-shift equivalent over \(\mathbb Z_+\) if and only if \(b\mid n\) or \(c\mid n\). In particular, the displayed \((b,c)=(5,4)\) family is elementary exactly for parameters divisible by 4 or 5.
limitations: The theorem classifies one-step (elementary) SSE only; it does not decide whether non-elementary SSE exists when neither divisibility condition holds.
All entries are positive and the nonsingularity condition \(n^2\ne bc\) is essential to the proof through invertibility of the elementary factors.
No claim is made for arbitrary two-by-two nonnegative matrix pairs.
